title: Karachi Planting Guide: 1. The one thing to understand: salt decides what grows
text: In Karachi, salt decides what grows, not heat. The city never gets cold, so no plant dies of frost, and almost every plant can handle the temperature. What actually kills plants here is salt in the soil, salt in the water, poor drainage and bad irrigation water. The system must therefore check salt first and everything else after. Most plant apps in the world do it the other way round, which is why they do not work in Karachi.

title: Karachi Planting Guide: 2. What Karachi is like for plants
text: - Rainfall: about 310 mm a year, and 77% of it falls in July–August. Every planting needs irrigation. - Temperature: normally 13 °C to 35 °C. It never freezes. There are two hot peaks, in May and in October. - Record heat: 47.8 °C. Heat waves happen; the 2015 heat wave killed over 1,200 people. - Humidity: 45% in winter and 70% in the monsoon. High humidity causes fungus and disease on vegetables. - Soil: sandy, pH 7.4–7.9, i.e. alkaline, not acidic. - Lime in soil: 13% to 31%. The soil is very chalky, which blocks iron and zinc, so leaves turn yellow. - Salt-affected land in Sindh: 2.6 million hectares; nearly half of the surveyed land in Sindh has a salt problem. - Green cover in Karachi: about 1%, against a recommended minimum of 25%, so there is a lot of room to plant.

title: Karachi Planting Guide: 3. Four kinds of sites
text: Every location falls into one of four site types, and each has a different main problem. - Coastal (Hawke's Bay, Clifton, Korangi Creek, Ibrahim Hyderi). Main problem: salt in the soil and salt in the sea air. What works: mangrove, peelu, farash, Pongamia, Casuarina. - Dense urban (Saddar, Lyari, Gulshan, road medians). Main problem: no root space, heat and pollution. What works: tough shade trees, or pots if space is small. - Peri-urban farm (Gadap, Malir, Memon Goth). Main problem: irrigation water quality. What works: vegetables, fruit trees and fodder. - Inland dry land (Kirthar foothills, open Gadap). Main problem: not enough water. What works: native desert trees and range grasses.

title: Karachi Planting Guide: 4. Six things that kill plants in Karachi
text: 1. Salt in the soil. This is the biggest one. It is measured as ECe; above 4 dS/m most normal vegetables start losing yield. 2. Sodic soil. This is different from salty soil: the soil goes hard and water will not soak in. It needs gypsum, not just washing. Washing a sodic soil without gypsum makes it worse. 3. Bad irrigation water. This is the one everybody misses. Water can pass a normal salt test and still ruin the soil. The hidden number is RSC; above 2.5 the water is not fit for irrigation. 4. No drainage. If water cannot drain away, salt builds up instead of washing out. A well-drained salty site is better than a badly drained, slightly salty one. 5. No root space. A tree in a 1.2 m² pavement hole will die no matter which species is picked. Check space before checking anything else. 6. Not enough watering at the start. Most failures are this. A tree that needs three years of watering will die with someone who waters twice a week, whatever its salt tolerance.

title: Karachi Planting Guide: 5. What we need to know about a site (8 questions)
text: The input form needs nothing more than these questions: 1. Where is it? (drop a pin on the map) 2. How big is the area, and is it ground, a raised bed or a pot? 3. How deep can roots go before hitting rock, rubble or a slab? 4. How many hours of direct sun does it get? 5. Where does the water come from, and how many days a week can you water? 6. What do you want: food, shade, screening, flowers, habitat or fodder? 7. How much care can you give: daily, a few times a week, or rarely? 8. Do you have a soil test? If there is no soil test, three simple questions are asked instead: Is there a white crust on the dry soil? What grows there already without watering? Has anything died after seeming to settle in? These answers give a rough guess only, never a confident answer.

title: Karachi Planting Guide: 6. What to plant
text: The full report covers about 65 plants. Short version by group: - Vegetables and field crops. Good choices: barley, cotton, sorghum, guar, wheat, cowpea, beetroot, zucchini, bermuda grass. Risky: tomato, cucumber, spinach, cabbage, okra, chilli, brinjal. Avoid on salty soil: lettuce, onion, beans. - Fruit trees. Good choices: date palm, guava, chikoo, ber, pomegranate, jamun. Need good soil and water: banana, mango, coconut, papaya. Poor in Karachi: orange, grape. - Shade and street trees. Good choices: neem, Pongamia (sukhchain), babul, kandi, siris, arjun, jangli badam, amaltas, Casuarina. Only with big root space: peepal, banyan. Do not plant: Conocarpus, gulmohar. - Coastal and salty sites. Good choices: mangrove (tidal areas only), peelu, farash, Cordia, kirir, saltbush, moringa. Prosopis juliflora works but spreads and becomes a weed. - Flowers and ground cover. Good choices: bougainvillea, Dodonaea, henna, jasmine, aloe vera, bermuda grass. Oleander is poisonous and must not be planted where children or animals can reach it. On Conocarpus: it makes up 62% of Karachi's street trees and was banned in 2016, and KMC is already replacing it with neem. It damages pipes and drains, uses a lot of water and causes pollen allergy, so the system must not recommend it.

title: Karachi Planting Guide: 7. How the system should decide
text: Three simple steps, in this order: 1. Remove what cannot survive. Plants that are too salt-sensitive for the site, need more root space than there is, are poisonous where children play, or need more watering than the user can give are thrown out completely. A good score elsewhere cannot save them. 2. Score what is left, out of 100. Salt gets the most weight (22%), then water need (18%), then temperature (14%), then soil, space, care, purpose, lime and wind. 3. Say how sure we are. High means lab results are available, Medium means partly tested, and Low means the answer is a guess from the type of site. At Low confidence no number is shown, only the test that would fix it. Always tell the user why: both why a plant was chosen and why one was rejected, with the actual number that caused it. Farmers and agronomists check the rejections first.

title: Karachi Planting Guide: 8. Three worked examples (part 1)
text: These examples use made-up site values to show how the system works; they are not measurements from real places. - A. Coastal plot near Hawke's Bay. The soil is very salty (ECe 11.4) and water comes by tanker twice a week. Almost all vegetables and fruit trees are out. Recommended: peelu, Pongamia and farash, with a Casuarina windbreak on the sea side. The real risk is not salt but finding enough water for the first three years. - B. Tree pit in Saddar. A 1.2 m² hole in the pavement with concrete 60 cm down and no soil test. Peepal, banyan and gulmohar are rejected straight away because the hole is too small; no test is needed for that. Neem and Pongamia are possible, but nobody can be sure without a soil test. Honest answer: make the hole bigger first, then test the soil.

title: Karachi Planting Guide: 8. Three worked examples (part 2)
text: - C. Farm in Gadap. The soil is moderately salty and the borewell water has an RSC of 3.1, above the safe limit. Date palm, guava, sorghum, cowpea and beetroot all work well. Tomato will lose about a quarter of its yield. Onion, orange and beans are out. The real advice is to fix the water first with gypsum and add extra water for leaching; otherwise, within a few seasons, even the good crops will start failing.

title: Karachi Planting Guide: 9. Tests we should get done
text: Two cheap test panels turn a guess into a real answer. Minimum soil test: - ECe (salt level): the single most important number; nothing works without it. - pH: shows lime and sodic problems. - Texture (sand, silt or clay): affects drainage and watering. - SAR or sodium: shows whether washing the soil will work or make it worse. - Lime (CaCO3): explains yellow leaves and locked-up nutrients. - Organic matter: soil health and water holding. Minimum water test: - EC and pH: basic salt level of the water. - Sodium, calcium and magnesium: needed to calculate SAR. - Carbonate and bicarbonate: needed to calculate RSC, the number everyone forgets. - Chloride and boron: cause leaf burn and toxicity. - Heavy metals: only if the water comes from a drain or wastewater. How to sample: take 8–12 small scoops across the plot and mix them, and take two depths separately (0–30 cm and 30–60 cm). Sample at the end of the dry season, before the monsoon, when salt is at its highest. Do not mix a salty patch with clean soil; test them separately.

title: Karachi Planting Guide: 10. What we still do not know
text: - Okra: a major Karachi crop, with no published salt limit anywhere. - Chikoo: Karachi's biggest fruit crop by area (302 hectares), with no salt data at all. - Conocarpus: millions were planted because it is "salt tolerant", but nobody has ever published a number for it. - Vegetable planting dates for lower Sindh: no official Sindh calendar exists in public, so national dates are used as a rough guide. - Karachi groundwater salt levels: known to be brackish, but there are no reliable published figures. - Air quality: Karachi has no working public monitoring station, so pollution cannot be used as a hard rule, only as advice. None of these are guessed at in the system; they are shown as gaps, together with the test that would fill them.

title: Karachi Planting Guide: 11. The plan / 12. Bottom line
text: - Phase 1 (weeks 1–6): the 8 questions, the pass/fail rules, the first plant list and clear reasons for rejection. Before moving on, every rejection must name its rule and its source. - Phase 2 (weeks 7–14): scoring out of 100, confidence levels, and weather and soil data feeds. Before moving on, no score may be shown when the data is only a guess. - Phase 3 (weeks 15–26): soil and water test ordering, uploading results and unlocking full confidence. Target: 50 sites with real lab results. - Phase 4 (month 7 onwards): follow-up at 3, 12 and 36 months, learning from what lived and what died. Phase 1 is the one that has to be right. It needs no weather data, no scoring engine and no laboratory, and it already gives a recommendation that an expert can check and trust. Check salt first. Be honest when we do not know. Get people to test their soil. If we do those three things, the system will be more useful and more trusted than anything else available for Karachi.

title: Plantify FAQ: How does Plantify Karachi recommend plants?
text: Q: How does Plantify Karachi recommend plants? A: Plantify works in five steps. First, you give the location of your plot: GPS read from a photo, your current location, a pin on the map, or an area from the list. Second, the system finds the nearest of its 104 Karachi reference sites and uses that site's soil pH, texture, drainage, fertility, salinity and temperatures. Third, your answers to the site questions (signs of salt, watering days, space, care, purpose, and whether children or animals use the site) are combined with the site data. Fourth, a rule filter removes every one of the 85 candidate plants that cannot survive or is unsafe there, and each removed plant gets a reason. Fifth, the remaining plants are ranked by an XGBoost model, and the top 6 are shown with their scores, while the removed plants are listed with the reason each one was excluded.

title: Plantify FAQ: Which plants does the rule filter remove, and why?
text: Q: Which plants does the rule filter remove, and why? A: Before any scoring, a plant is removed completely if any one of these is true: it is on the do-not-plant list (for example Conocarpus, which is banned); it is poisonous and children or animals use the site; the site's salinity class is higher than the plant's salt tolerance; the soil pH is more than 1 unit outside the plant's absolute pH range; the coldest month is more than 3 °C below, or the hottest month more than 3 °C above, the plant's absolute temperature range; you can water fewer days than the plant needs (about 1, 3 or 7 days a week for low, medium or high water need, with one day of slack), or not at all when the plant needs more than low water; or the plant needs large root space and your space is not large. A good score elsewhere cannot bring a removed plant back.

title: Plantify FAQ: How is a plant's score out of 100 calculated?
text: Q: How is a plant's score out of 100 calculated? A: Plants that pass the filter get a rule score out of 100 built from eleven parts. The weights are: salt 22, water 18, temperature 14, soil pH 8, space 8, purpose 8, care 6, soil texture 4, drainage 4, fertility 4, and pollution and urban heat 4. Each part is a fraction between 0 and 1 of its weight; for example, a plant whose salt tolerance is at least one class above the site's salinity gets the full salt weight, and one that only just tolerates it gets 70% of it. Bonuses are then added: +5 if the plant is native, +5 if the Karachi planting guide rates it good, and +3 if it is proven in Karachi. The score is capped at 100. A plant counts as suitable when it passes the filter and scores 70 or more; these labels are what the model was trained on.

title: Plantify FAQ: What does the XGBoost model do, and why use it if the labels come from rules?
text: Q: What does the XGBoost model do, and why use it if the labels come from rules? A: The XGBoost model takes 66 features for each site, user answers and plant, and predicts the probability that the plant is suitable. Plantify ranks plants by this probability. The training labels came from the planting guide's rule engine, so the model learns to reproduce those rules; its very high accuracy shows fidelity to the rules, not proof that plants survive in the field. The project gives four reasons for using it anyway: many plants tie at the 100-point cap and the rule engine can only break ties by list order, while the model gives a continuous probability; the model has smooth boundaries instead of hard cutoffs such as pH 6.49 versus 6.50; it predicts in milliseconds; and it can later be retrained on real survival data collected in FYP-2.

title: Plantify FAQ: What data was the model trained on?
text: Q: What data was the model trained on? A: There is no database of planting outcomes for Karachi, so the project built 221,000 training scenarios: 104 Karachi reference sites × 25 user answer profiles × 85 candidate plants. Each row combines 10 site features, 6 user answers and 33 plant traits; 7 categorical features are one-hot encoded, giving 66 columns, and missing traits are filled with -1. The target is "suitable" (1) or "unsuitable" (0), labelled by the planting guide's rule engine. The data was split by site, not by random rows, so the test sites were never seen in training: 176,375 rows from 83 sites for training and 44,625 rows from 21 unseen sites for testing.

title: Plantify FAQ: How well does the model perform, and how does XGBoost compare with Random Forest?
text: Q: How well does the model perform, and how does XGBoost compare with Random Forest? A: On the 21 unseen test sites, XGBoost scored accuracy 0.99987, precision 0.99975, recall 0.99995, F1 0.99985 and ROC-AUC 0.99999993. Its confusion matrix has 24,299 true negatives, 5 false positives, 1 false negative and 20,320 true positives. The Random Forest baseline had accuracy 0.9985 with 69 errors, against 7 errors for XGBoost. Top-6 overlap with the rule engine's ranking was 0.506 for XGBoost and 0.44 for Random Forest; the overlap is limited because many plants tie at the 100-point cap and the rule engine breaks those ties by list order. XGBoost was chosen for the backend. These numbers show the model reproduces the rules, not real-world survival.

title: Plantify FAQ: Which factors matter most to the model?
text: Q: Which factors matter most to the model? A: By XGBoost feature importance, the ten most important features are: the plant's maximum optimal pH (0.1505), whether the plant is on the do-not-plant list (0.1452), the site's salinity (0.1114), the plant's salt tolerance (0.1068), whether the plant needs large space (0.0898), the plant's water need (0.0753), whether the user's space is large (0.0567), whether the planting guide rates the plant good (0.0386), the number of days the user can water (0.0365), and whether the plant is low maintenance (0.0319). Salinity and salt tolerance together are among the strongest drivers, which matches the planting guide's message that salt decides what grows in Karachi.

title: Plantify FAQ: Where does the site, salinity and climate data come from?
text: Q: Where does the site, salinity and climate data come from? A: Each of the 104 reference sites has soil data from SoilGrids 2.0 (pH, clay, sand, organic carbon and bulk density), plus texture, drainage and fertility classes. Salinity starts from the ISRIC Global Soil Salinity Map 2016 (Ivushkin et al. 2019, 250 m resolution, validation accuracy 67–70%). Version 2.4 projects salinity to 2026 using the damped trend of the ISRIC maps for 2005, 2009 and 2016, and never sets it below the 2016 value. Climate uses 10-year averages; the urban heat measure uses the hottest-month mean air temperature for 2015–2024 as a proxy, not satellite land-surface temperature. The 85 plants come from the team's species file, Karachi research papers and the EcoCrop database.

title: Plantify FAQ: How is the salinity of my plot decided?
text: Q: How is the salinity of my plot decided? A: Salinity is a class from 0 to 2: low, medium or high. Every reference site has a default class from the 2026 salinity projection. In the 2026 projection, 62 of the 104 sites are saline (class 1), up from 43 in 2016, because salinity in Karachi has been rising. Your answers can raise your plot's class but never lower it. The four signs are a white crust on the soil, salty borewell water, burnt leaf edges on nearby plants, and being within 2 km of the sea. One "yes" raises salinity to at least medium. Three "yes" answers, or two on a site that is already saline on the map, raise it to high. Salinity matters because a plant whose salt tolerance is below your plot's class is removed outright.

title: Plantify FAQ: Why does salinity matter so much in Karachi?
text: Q: Why does salinity matter so much in Karachi? A: The project's planting guide says that in Karachi salt decides what grows, not heat: the city never freezes, so almost every plant can handle the temperature, but salt in the soil and water, poor drainage and bad irrigation water kill plants. Plantify therefore checks salt first. Salt has the largest weight in the score (22 of 100), a plant less salt tolerant than the site is removed before scoring, and site salinity and plant salt tolerance are among the model's four most important features. Salinity is also rising: in the 2026 projection 62 of the 104 reference sites are saline, compared with 43 in 2016.

title: Plantify FAQ: What are the limitations of Plantify's recommendations?
text: Q: What are the limitations of Plantify's recommendations? A: First, the training labels come from the planting guide's rules, not from records of which plants actually survived, so the model's accuracy shows that it follows the rules, not that plants will live. Second, 31 of the 85 plants have estimated traits taken from general horticultural references rather than measurements (23 with medium and 8 with low confidence), and they need expert checking. Third, your plot is matched to the nearest of 104 reference sites, which can be several kilometres away, so local soil may differ. Fourth, the salinity map has 250 m resolution and 67–70% validation accuracy, and the 2026 projection is an estimate. Fifth, the heat measure is a proxy from air temperature. A soil test gives a more reliable answer than any of these estimates.

title: Plantify FAQ: How does the Plantify chat assistant answer questions?
text: Q: How does the Plantify chat assistant answer questions? A: The assistant uses retrieval-augmented generation. Plantify's species data, site data, the Karachi planting guide and this FAQ are split into short passages. Each passage is turned into a vector with the BGE-small embedding model and stored in a FAISS index. When you ask a question, it is embedded the same way, the most similar passages are retrieved (with extra weight for your own recommended plants and your own site), and the Gemini model writes an answer using only those passages and your current recommendation. It names the sources it used. If the information is not in Plantify's data, it says so instead of guessing. No model was fine-tuned.
